source_text:
Considera denique sacra ipsa et ipsa mysteria: inuenies exitus tristes, fata et funera et luctus atque planctus miserorum deorum. Isis perditum filium cum Cynocephalo suo et caluis sacerdotibus luget, plangit, inquirit, et Isiaci miseri caedunt pectora et dolorem infelicissimae matris imitantur: mox inuento paruulo gaudet Isis, . exultant sacerdotes, Cynocephalus inuentor gloriatur, nec desinunt annis omnibus uel perdere quod inueniunt uel inuenire quod perdunt.
nonne ridiculum est uel lugere quod colas uel colere quod lugeas? haec tamen Aegyptia quondam nunc et sacra Romana sunt. Ceres facibus accensis et serpente circumdata errore subreptam et corruptam Liberam anxia et sollicita uestigat: haec sunt Eleusinia. et quae Iouis sacra sunt?
nutrix capella est et auido patri subtrahitur infans, ne uoretur, et Corybantum cymbalis, ne pater audiat uagitus, tinnitus eliditur.
Cybelae Dindyma pudet dicere, quae adulterum suum infeliciter placitum, quoniam ipsa et deformis et uetula, ut multorum deorum mater, ad stuprum inlicere non poterat, exsecuit, ut deum scilicet faceret eunuchum. propter hanc fabulam Galli eam et semiuiri sui corporis supplicio colunt. haec iam non sunt sacra, tormenta sunt.
quid? formae ipsae et habitus nonne arguunt ludibria et dedecora deorum uestrorum? Vulcanus claudus deus et debilis, Apollo tot aetatibus leuis, Aesculapius bene barbatus, etsi semper adulescentis Apollinis filius, Neptunus glaucis oculis, Minerua caesiis, bubulis Iuno, pedibus Mercurius alatis, Pan ungulatis, Saturnus compeditis. Ianus uero frontes duas gestat, quasi et auersus incedat: Diana interim est alte succincta uenatrix et Ephesia mammis multis et uberibus exstructa et Triuia trinis capitibus et multis manibus horrifica.
quid ipse Iuppiter uester? modo inberbis statuitur, modo barbatus locatur; et cum Hammon dicitur, habet cornua, et cum Capitolinus, tunc gerit fulmina, et cum Latiaris, cruore perfunditur, et cum Feretrius, t non auditur. et ne longius multos Ioues obeam, tot sunt Iouis monstra quot nomina.
Erigone suspensa de laqueo est, ut uirgo inter astra ignita sit, Castores alternis moriuntur ut uiuant, Aesculapius ut in deum surgat fulminatur, Hercules ut hominem exuat, Oetaeis ignibus concrematur.
thought_title: Pagan rites and gods are mourning, mutilation, and mockery
orientation: Octavius is continuing his attack on the pagan gods, now turning from their births and deaths to their rites and images.
pass_a_gloss: Consider finally the rites themselves and the mysteries themselves: you will find sad outcomes, deaths and funerals and griefs and lamentations of wretched gods. Isis mourns, beats her breast, and searches for her lost son with her dog-headed god and her bald priests, and the wretched worshippers of Isis beat their breasts and imitate the grief of the most unhappy mother: soon Isis rejoices at the found little one, the priests exult, the dog-headed finder boasts, and they do not cease every year either to lose what they find or to find what they lose. Is it not ridiculous either to mourn what you worship or to worship what you mourn? Yet these things once Egyptian are now also Roman rites. Ceres with torches lit and encircled by a serpent anxiously and anxiously tracks Libera, stolen away and corrupted through wandering: these are the Eleusinian rites. And what are the rites of Jupiter? His nurse is a she-goat, and the infant is snatched away from his greedy father so that he is not devoured, and the ringing is struck out by the cymbals of the Corybantes so that the father does not hear the wailing. It shames me to tell the Dindyma of Cybele, who cut off her lover, unhappily pleasing, since she herself, both ugly and old, as mother of many gods, could not entice him to defilement, so that she might make him a god, evidently a eunuch. Because of this story the Galli worship her also by the punishment of their own half-male body. These things are no longer rites, they are tortures. What? Do not the very shapes and appearances prove the mockeries and disgraces of your gods? Vulcan is a lame and crippled god, Apollo beardless through so many ages, Aesculapius well bearded, although always the son of youthful Apollo, Neptune with gray eyes, Minerva with gray-green eyes, Juno with ox eyes, Mercury with winged feet, Pan with hoofed feet, Saturn with fettered feet. Janus indeed wears two faces, as if he walks also turned backward: Diana meanwhile is a huntress girt up high, and the Ephesian Diana is built up with many breasts and udders, and Trivia is horrifying with three heads and many hands. What of your Jupiter himself? Now he is set up beardless, now he is placed bearded; and when he is called Hammon, he has horns, and when he is called Capitolinus, then he carries thunderbolts, and when he is called Latiaris, he is drenched with blood, and when he is called Feretrius, he is not heard. And not to go through many Jupiters at greater length, there are as many monsters of Jupiter as names. Erigone is hung from a noose, so that she might be a virgin set on fire among the stars, the Castors die in turns so that they may live, Aesculapius is struck by lightning so that he may rise into a god, Hercules is burned up by the fires of Oeta so that he may put off the man.

choices.why: Keeps the paradox of gods who suffer, which is Octavius's point.
Renders the compound literally so the absurdity is visible.
Superlative kept to match the mock pathos of the rite.
Stuprum is sexual dishonor; 'defilement' keeps the moral charge without modernizing.
Both nouns kept as a pair to preserve the rhetorical doubling.

choices.english: so that he may put off the man
choices.why: Literal rendering of exuere hominem, keeping the metaphor of stripping off humanity.
rejected: so that he may cease to be a man

pass_b_english: Consider, finally, the sacred rites and the mysteries themselves. You will find sad outcomes: deaths, funerals, griefs, and lamentations of wretched gods. Isis mourns her lost son with her dog-headed god and her bald priests. She wails, she searches, and the miserable worshippers of Isis beat their breasts and imitate the grief of that most unhappy mother. Then, when the little one is found, Isis rejoices, the priests exult, the dog-headed god boasts as the finder, and they do not stop losing what they find or finding what they lose year after year. Is it not ridiculous either to mourn what you worship or to worship what you mourn? Yet these rites, once Egyptian, are now also Roman.

Ceres, with torches lit and a serpent coiled around her, anxiously and restlessly tracks Libera, who was snatched away and defiled in her wandering. These are the Eleusinian rites. And what are the sacred rites of Jupiter? His nurse is a she-goat, and the infant is hidden from his greedy father so that he will not be devoured, and the ringing of the Corybantes' cymbals drowns out his wailing so that his father will not hear it.

I am ashamed to speak of Cybele on Mount Dindyma. She cut off her adulterer, who had pleased her only unhappily, because she herself, both ugly and old, as the mother of many gods, could not entice him to defilement. She did it, of course, to make him a eunuch god. Because of this story the Galli, her eunuch priests, worship her and punish their own bodies by castrating themselves. These are no longer sacred rites; they are tortures.

What of the forms and appearances themselves? Do they not expose the mockeries and disgraces of your gods? Vulcan is a lame and crippled god. Apollo is smooth-faced through so many ages. Aesculapius has a fine beard, though he is always the son of the youthful Apollo. Neptune has gray-green eyes, Minerva blue-gray, Juno ox-eyes, Mercury winged feet, Pan hoofed feet, Saturn shackled feet. Janus indeed wears two faces, as if he walked backwards. Diana, meanwhile, is a huntress girt up high, and the Ephesian Diana is built up with many breasts and teats, and Trivia, the three-formed goddess, is horrifying with three heads and many hands.

What of your Jupiter himself? Now he is set up beardless, now he is placed bearded. When he is called Hammon, he has horns. When he is called Capitoline, then he wields thunderbolts. When he is called Latiaris, he is drenched in blood. When he is called Feretrius, he does not hear. And not to go through many Jupiters at length, there are as many monstrosities of Jupiter as there are names.

Erigone is hung from a noose, so that as a virgin she may be set among the stars. The Castors die in turns so that they may live. Aesculapius is struck by lightning so that he may rise as a god. Hercules is burned in the fires of Oeta so that he may put off the man.

polish.changed: Clarified who is speaking and acting, identified obscure figures like the Galli and Trivia, smoothed sentence order, and removed translationese while preserving every claim and reference.

notes.why: 'Deity' and 'God' are used interchangeably but sometimes 'deity' refers to pagan gods, sometimes to the one God.
notes.fix: Distinguish pagan 'deities' from the one 'God' more consistently.

notes.quote: so that she might make him a eunuch god, of course. Because of this story the Galli worship her and punish their own bodies by becoming half-male
notes.why: 'half-male' is unclear; refers to castrated state, but 'half-male' is not standard English.
'Dindyma' seems to mean the shrine/mountain, but used for the goddess herself; confusing.

notes.quote: I am ashamed to speak of the Dindyma of Cybele
notes.why: Dindyma (the mountain associated with Cybele) is an obscure term.
notes.fix: Gloss: Dindyma, the mountain sacred to Cybele.

notes.quote: the Galli worship her and punish their own bodies by becoming half-male
notes.why: Galli (eunuch priests of Cybele) are not identified.
notes.fix: Gloss: the Galli, eunuch priests of Cybele.

notes.quote: Trivia is horrifying with three heads
notes.why: Trivia (an epithet of Diana/Hecate) is unexplained.
notes.fix: Gloss: Trivia, an epithet of Hecate/Diana as goddess of crossroads.
